heading: Worked examples
quote: Publicness is judged on the **entire bucket policy**, so a single `"Principal": "*"` statement makes the policy public and `RestrictPublicBuckets` then strips out the **named** cross-account grants too.

signal: must have an audit trail of who used the encryption key, or a key policy, or cross-account access to encrypted data
answer: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key
against: SSE-S3 — it encrypts everything but gives no key policy and no per-use trail of the key
heading: Which encryption options actually exist — per service
quote: | **SSE-KMS** (`aws:kms`) | your KMS key | you need an **audit trail of key use** and a **key policy** — the compliance answer |

signal: each file must be encrypted with a different key, without the overhead of splitting the data into logical groups
answer: Plain SSE-S3 — it already encrypts every object under its own unique key
against: SSE-KMS with per-object encryption context, or separate buckets per logical group — both are the over-built answer to uniqueness S3 already provides
heading: Which encryption options actually exist — per service
quote: is answered by one bucket with plain **SSE-S3** — no key management, no per-chunk buckets, no KMS bill.

signal: high-throughput SSE-KMS workload, KMS request charges too high, must keep the audit trail
answer: Enable S3 Bucket Keys (objects stay SSE-KMS)
against: Switching to SSE-S3 or SSE-C — also cheaper, but it abandons the key policy and CloudTrail trail that made SSE-KMS the requirement
heading: Which encryption options actually exist — per service
quote: The fix is **S3 Bucket Keys** — a short-lived bucket-level key that cuts KMS

signal: default encryption has just been turned on — what happens to the objects already in the bucket?
answer: Nothing; rewrite them with S3 Batch Operations → Copy
against: Assuming default encryption re-encrypts in place — it is a rule applied at write time only
heading: Worked examples
quote: Default encryption applies to **new** objects only. Existing objects keep their previous encryption until you rewrite them — **S3 Batch Operations → Copy**.

signal: temporary access to one private object served DIRECTLY FROM S3
answer: A presigned URL, which carries the permissions of whoever generated it
against: Creating an IAM user for them, or making the bucket public — the first builds a permanent identity for a one-off, the second exposes everything
heading: Worked examples
quote: It uses **the generator's**. That's why it works for someone with no AWS account at all

signal: how long can a presigned URL be valid for?
answer: 7 days (604800s) via CLI/SDK; 12 hours via the console
against: Quoting one number — the console ceiling is 12 hours, so a stem that says 'generated in the console' caps at 12h not 7 days
heading: Presigned URLs
quote: Max expiry: **7 days (604800s)** via CLI/SDK, **12 hours** via the console.

signal: immutable, nobody may delete it, not even us — and the protected things are S3 OBJECT VERSIONS
answer: Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode
against: GOVERNANCE mode — identical mechanics, but anyone with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention plus the bypass header can delete, so it fails a 'not even root' requirement
heading: Object Lock (WORM) — verified 2026-08
quote: **COMPLIANCE mode** — *"a protected object version can't be overwritten or deleted by any user, including the root user"*

signal: WORM protection wanted, but a named admin group must keep an emergency override
answer: Object Lock in GOVERNANCE mode plus s3:BypassGovernanceRetention and the x-amz-bypass-governance-retention header
against: COMPLIANCE mode — there is no override at all; AWS's only documented escape before expiry is closing the account
heading: Object Lock (WORM) — verified 2026-08
quote: **GOVERNANCE mode** — overridable by a principal with **`s3:BypassGovernanceRetention`** plus the `x-amz-bypass-governance-retention:true` header.

signal: an object in a WORM/Object Lock bucket 'disappeared' and the delete call returned 200 OK
answer: A simple DELETE (no version id) added a delete marker; the locked version is intact underneath
against: Concluding the lock failed — a DELETE naming the protected version id returns 403 AccessDenied, which is the lock working
heading: Object Lock (WORM) — verified 2026-08
quote: a **permanent** `DELETE` (with a version id) → **403 AccessDenied**; a **simple** `DELETE` (no version id) → **200 OK and a delete marker**.

signal: require MFA before a version can be permanently deleted or versioning turned off
answer: MFA Delete — enabled only by the bucket-owning root account with an MFA device, via the CLI or the API/SDKs
against: 'CLI only' / an IAM admin doing it in the console — the console cannot do it at all, but an API/SDK option is valid, so don't reject an answer that says PutBucketVersioning
heading: MFA Delete
quote: Requires the **root** account that owns the bucket, with an MFA device. Configurable via the **CLI or the API/SDKs** — **never the console**, and never by an IAM user.

signal: one bucket shared by many teams, each needing its own permissions / bucket policy hitting the 20 KB limit
answer: S3 Access Points — a named endpoint per team, each with its own policy and optional VPC restriction
against: One large bucket policy — it hits the 20 KB ceiling and becomes unreviewable; note an access point can only narrow, never grant what the bucket withholds
heading: Two policies pointing at each other
quote: Bucket policies have a **20 KB** ceiling, and when one bucket is shared by many teams the answer is **Access Points**

signal: partner account is granted s3:GetObject in the bucket policy and still gets AccessDenied
answer: Cross-account needs both sides — their IAM policy must also allow the call
against: Widening the bucket policy further — the missing half lives in an account you do not control
heading: Worked examples
quote: Cross-account access needs **both sides**: your bucket policy must allow their principal **and** their IAM policy must allow the call.

signal: Windows EC2 instances need a shared file system, with Active Directory users and Windows ACLs
answer: FSx for Windows File Server (SMB + AD + Windows ACLs)
against: EFS — 'shared file system' fits perfectly in words, but AWS does not support EFS with Windows EC2 instances, so it is an automatic elimination
heading: Traps
quote: **AWS does not support EFS with Windows EC2 instances.** Any question mentioning Windows, SMB, Active Directory, or Windows ACLs is pointing at **FSx for Windows File Server**

signal: one file system serving both Windows (SMB) and Linux (NFS) clients the same data
answer: FSx for NetApp ONTAP — the multi-protocol one
against: FSx for Windows File Server — Linux clients can speak SMB to it, but only ONTAP is the documented multi-protocol (NFS, SMB, iSCSI, NVMe) answer
heading: FSx: when the workload demands a *specific* file system
quote: **FSx for NetApp ONTAP** is **multi-protocol** — AWS lists *"NFS, SMB, **iSCSI** and **NVMe**"* — so it is the answer both when Linux and Windows clients need the same data

signal: low-latency *block* storage over iSCSI, with Multi-AZ high availability
answer: FSx for NetApp ONTAP — the only FSx flavour offering block over iSCSI
against: FSx for Windows File Server — the default 'lift-and-shift Windows' pick, but it is SMB *file* storage and offers no iSCSI block
heading: FSx: when the workload demands a *specific* file system
quote: so "iSCSI block + Multi-AZ HA" points at ONTAP and nothing else.

signal: HPC / ML training needs sub-millisecond POSIX access to a dataset that lives in S3
answer: FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket
against: EFS — a shared Linux file system, but it is not the speed/S3-backed-compute answer and has no S3 linkage
heading: FSx: when the workload demands a *specific* file system
quote: link a bucket and Lustre presents the objects in it as ordinary files, and can write results back.

signal: Lustre results must survive a file server failure / long-running job whose output can't be re-created
answer: Persistent deployment type (replicated, failed servers replaced)
against: Scratch — read as the 'cheaper and faster' choice, but the axis is durability: scratch is not replicated and the data does not survive a file server failure
heading: Traps
quote: The difference is **durability**, not performance. Scratch is **not replicated** and does not survive a file server failure; persistent is replicated with automatic server replacement.

signal: stop the on-premises storage footprint from growing, keep hot data local
answer: Volume Gateway — cached volumes (primary copy in S3)
against: Stored volumes — the names are nearly interchangeable; anchor on which copy is authoritative, and 'reduce on-prem storage' means the primary must live in S3
heading: Traps
quote: **Cached** = primary in S3, hot subset local — chosen to stop on-premises storage growing. **Stored** = primary on-premises, snapshots to S3

signal: low-latency on-premises access to the *entire* dataset, plus offsite backups
answer: Volume Gateway — stored volumes (all data local, snapshots to S3)
against: Cached volumes — only a hot subset is local, so 'the entire dataset at low latency' fails
heading: Storage Gateway: making cloud storage look local
quote: The tell: *"reduce on-premises storage footprint"* → **cached**. *"low-latency access to the entire dataset"* / *"offsite backup"* → **stored**.

signal: existing backup software must keep writing to tape, unchanged
answer: Tape Gateway (a virtual tape library)
against: DataSync — it transfers data and the job ends; the backup software needs a permanent local interface, which is what a gateway is
heading: Traps
quote: "Our backup software must keep writing to tape" → Tape Gateway.

signal: migrate or sync on-premises NFS/SMB data to AWS on a schedule, with integrity validation
answer: AWS DataSync
against: Storage Gateway — also network-based and also needs something installed locally, but it is a permanent bridge the on-prem system keeps using, not a transfer job
heading: Traps
quote: **DataSync transfers data** — a migration or a scheduled sync, after which the job is done. **Storage Gateway is a permanent bridge**

signal: process or filter the data where it is collected, before or instead of shipping it
answer: Snowball Edge Compute Optimized
against: Snowball Edge Storage Optimized — the bigger device (210 TB vs 28 TB), so 'more capability' reads as the right answer; Compute Optimized is the configuration AWS designates for compute
heading: Which Snow device — storage volume, or compute at the edge?
quote: | to **process data where it is collected** before or instead of shipping it | **Snowball Edge Compute Optimized** | same 104 vCPU / 416 GB, but **28 TB** — the storage is sacrificed for compute |

signal: centrally managed backups copied into a *different AWS account*
answer: AWS Backup cross-account copy — which requires an AWS Organizations structure
against: Cross-Region copy — the answer when the requirement is distance from production, not account isolation; only cross-account pulls in Organizations
heading: AWS Backup: one place instead of six
quote: **Cross-account copy**, which requires **AWS Organizations**

signal: immutable, nobody may delete it, not even us — and the protected things are RECOVERY POINTS IN A BACKUP VAULT
answer: AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode
against: Governance mode — it can be unlocked by anyone holding the IAM permission, so it fails an 'immutable even to us' requirement
heading: AWS Backup: one place instead of six
quote: **Governance mode** can be unlocked by anyone with the IAM permission; **compliance mode** cannot be, by anyone including AWS, once its grace time (minimum 3 days) expires.

signal: Auto Scaling instances across several AZs must all see the same uploaded files
answer: EFS, with a mount target in each AZ the ASG spans
against: One shared EBS volume — an EBS volume lives in a single AZ and attaches to one instance, so it cannot back an ASG spanning AZs
heading: Worked examples
quote: The fix is **EFS**: create the file system, create a **mount target in each AZ** the ASG spans

signal: an EFS file that moved to IA is accessed again — does it return to Standard?
answer: No, not by default; you must set the Transition into Standard policy to on-first-access
against: Assuming automatic promotion like a cache — the default is None, and unlike Glacier there is no restore job either
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: **Transition into Standard defaults to *None*** — an accessed file does **not** come back automatically

signal: "must remain available if an entire Availability Zone fails" / "no data loss on failover"
answer: RDS Multi-AZ (synchronous standby, automatic DNS failover)
against: A read replica — it is asynchronous and promotion is manual, so it is read scaling, not HA.
heading: Multi-AZ and read replicas are two different jobs
quote: **Multi-AZ** keeps a **synchronous** standby in another AZ.

signal: "offload reporting/BI queries off production at the lowest cost"
answer: A same-Region read replica (in another AZ) — replication traffic is free
against: A cross-Region replica: that one is billed as inter-Region transfer, and is only right when the requirement is DR or readers in another geography. A same-AZ replica buys nothing either — the cross-AZ charge does not apply to replication.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: - **Read-replica replication is free within the same Region**, across AZs included; **cross-Region** replication is billed as inter-Region data transfer.

signal: "upgrade the database engine version with minimal downtime"
answer: Blue/green deployment
against: Multi-AZ — it protects against failure, not a planned engine upgrade; both primary and standby get upgraded.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: *"Database engine upgrades require downtime… You can minimize the downtime required for DB instance upgrade by using a **blue/green deployment**."*

signal: "an existing, running, unencrypted database must now be encrypted at rest"
answer: Snapshot → copy the snapshot with encryption enabled → restore the copy (new instance, new endpoint)
against: "Modify the DB instance and enable encryption" — encryption at rest is a creation-time-only property, so that option does not exist.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: *"You can only encrypt an Amazon RDS DB instance when you create it, not after"*

signal: "remove hard-coded database credentials" / "the application should authenticate using its IAM role, with no password stored"
answer: Enable IAM database authentication (then `rds-db:connect` on the dbuser ARN)
against: "Attach an IAM role to the instance" or "restrict the security group to the app tier" offered on their own — a role is an identity control and an SG is a network control; neither authenticates to the engine, and the feature is off by default.
heading: Worked examples
quote: **names the feature**: *enable IAM database authentication*.

signal: "database users must sign in with their existing corporate / Active Directory credentials" / "single sign-on to the database"
answer: Kerberos authentication with AWS Managed Microsoft AD
against: IAM database authentication (that is a signed token, not corporate SSO) and Secrets Manager (that is still password auth). Also note Kerberos is unsupported on MariaDB, so a MariaDB stem is not this.
heading: 07 – RDS & Aurora
quote: **Kerberos/AD answers "log in with existing corporate credentials / SSO"** (not MariaDB).

signal: "about 15 minutes after each deploy, NEW database connections fail while existing connections keep working"
answer: The IAM auth token was minted once at startup and cached as the password — generate it inside the connection factory
against: "The database is failing over" or "max_connections exhausted" — those break existing connections too; the giveaway is that open sessions are unaffected.
heading: Worked examples
quote: the connection pool minted **one** token at startup and cached it as "the password."

signal: "thousands of concurrent Lambda executions exhaust the database's connections"
answer: RDS Proxy
against: Adding read replicas or a bigger instance class — more capacity does not stop each concurrent execution from opening its own connection.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: **RDS Proxy** (connection pooling for Lambda/serverless)

signal: "migrate SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal application code changes" with Babelfish and SCT+DMS both listed as options
answer: Both — Babelfish for the application's T-SQL/driver, SCT + DMS for schema and data (a Select TWO)
against: Picking just one: Babelfish alone leaves an empty database; SCT+DMS alone leaves every query to be rewritten. Also eliminate Glue "converting T-SQL" and a custom endpoint "emulating SQL Server".
heading: Worked examples
quote: this is almost always a **Select TWO**, which is why picking one feels right and scores zero.

signal: "see how individual processes or threads on the DB instance are using CPU and memory"
answer: Enhanced Monitoring (agent inside the instance → CloudWatch Logs, `RDSOSMetrics`)
against: Standard CloudWatch metrics — `CPUUtilization`, `FreeableMemory`, `DatabaseConnections` are hypervisor-level and available with Enhanced Monitoring off; they describe the instance, not a process. Performance Insights answers "which query", not "which process".
heading: The three RDS monitoring layers (the one the exam confuses)
quote: | Stem trigger | "alert when CPU is high" | "see how **processes or threads** use the CPU" | "find the **query** causing the load" |

signal: "a full-size, isolated copy of production for staging, in minutes, at almost no extra storage cost" (Aurora)
answer: Aurora cloning (copy-on-write, up to 15 clones)
against: A snapshot restore physically copies every byte; Backtrack rewinds the source cluster instead of giving you a second one.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: - **Aurora cloning:** a new cluster sharing the source volume **copy-on-write** — ready in minutes, minimal extra storage, isolated from the source. **Up to 15** clones; the 16th is a **full copy**. Not a snapshot restore (copies bytes) and not Backtrack (rewinds the source).

signal: "unpredictable / intermittent / variable workload" + "minimize cost" on a relational database
answer: Aurora Serverless v2
against: A right-sized provisioned instance (idle hours still bill) — and plain RDS has no true serverless mode.
heading: Worked examples
quote: Trigger phrase: "unpredictable / intermittent / variable workload, minimize cost" → Aurora Serverless.

signal: "cross-Region DR / local reads in other Regions for an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster"
answer: Aurora Global Database (1 primary + up to 10 read-only Regions, sub-second replication)
against: A cross-Region Aurora Replica — that binlog-based option exists on Aurora MySQL only; Aurora PostgreSQL does not support it.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: *"Aurora PostgreSQL doesn't support cross-Region Aurora Replicas"*, so for Postgres the cross-Region answer is **Aurora Global Database** (up to 10 secondary Regions).

signal: "a single-instance Aurora cluster took ~10 minutes to recover" / "why was the failover so slow?"
answer: Add a reader instance in another AZ — with no reader there is nothing to promote, so Aurora must create a new primary
against: "Aurora isn't Multi-AZ, so redeploy on RDS Multi-AZ" — AWS applies the Multi-AZ term to Aurora directly; the real difference is that Aurora's second-AZ instance is a reader that doubles as the failover target.
heading: Worked examples
quote: and asking why failover was slow is asking for a **reader in another AZ**.

signal: "our Aurora bill is dominated by I/O charges" / "I/O is a quarter or more of Aurora spend"
answer: Switch the cluster to Aurora I/O-Optimized
against: Aurora Standard — it bills per million I/O requests and only wins below the ~25% threshold. Note you can move to I/O-Optimized only once every 30 days.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: *"the best choice when your I/O spending is 25% or more of your total Aurora database spending"*

signal: "friends-of-friends" / "fraud rings" / "queries that walk many relationships / multiple hops"
answer: Amazon Neptune (graph database)
against: Aurora — in SQL each hop is another join, so the query degrades as hops grow; Redshift is columnar analytics and OpenSearch is text search.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: **Multi-hop relationship traversal is a graph workload — that means Amazon Neptune**

signal: "move our MongoDB application to AWS with no application code change"
answer: Amazon DocumentDB (MongoDB-compatible)
against: DynamoDB — its API forces an application rewrite, so it fails the "no code change" requirement.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: *"you can run the same application code and use the same drivers and tools that you use with MongoDB"*

signal: "multi-threaded cache that can use all cores of a large node"
answer: Memcached
against: Redis — command execution is single-threaded (one core per node); it buys throughput with cluster-mode shards, not bigger boxes. This one gets remembered backwards.
heading: Redis is single-threaded — and that is not a bug
quote: **Redis executes commands single-threaded** — one core per node. **Memcached is the multi-threaded one.**

signal: "the client must discover all cache nodes automatically as nodes are added or removed" / "node discovery"
answer: Memcached with Auto Discovery (plus an ElastiCache client library that supports it)
against: Redis/Valkey — AWS states Auto Discovery is not available for them, so there is no Redis equivalent to muddy this signal. It outranks a Redis-sounding use case in the same stem.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: AWS explicitly states Auto Discovery is **not available for Valkey or Redis OSS**

signal: "user sessions must survive a cache node failure" / "data loss on node failure is unacceptable"
answer: Redis/Valkey (replication group, Multi-AZ auto-failover, persistence, backup)
against: Node-based Memcached — no replication, failover, persistence or backup, so a node loss loses the data. Scope it: if the stem names *Serverless* Memcached, do not eliminate it for lacking durability.
heading: What Memcached simply does not have
quote: anything you cannot afford to lose on a node failure belongs in Redis.

signal: "live top-100 leaderboard / ranking / real-time counter"
answer: Redis sorted sets
against: Memcached (simple key-value only) and a relational `ORDER BY score` over millions of rows per request.
heading: Worked examples
quote: Trigger words "leaderboard / ranking / real-time counter" → **Redis**.

signal: "microsecond reads for DynamoDB with no application rewrite"
answer: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) — API-compatible, swap the client
against: ElastiCache — it can cache anything but you would write your own cache-aside logic; it cannot front DynamoDB as a drop-in. Reverse the database and ElastiCache wins, since DAX cannot front a relational database at all.
heading: DAX — the cache that only fronts DynamoDB
quote: So "cache in front of DynamoDB with no application rewrite" is **DAX** — ElastiCache

signal: "strongly consistent reads are required" in a question that also offers a cache
answer: DAX does not help — a strongly consistent read passes straight through
against: Picking DAX on the strength of "microseconds" alone; consistency is the second discriminator and it eliminates DAX whatever else fits. DAX is also wrong for write-heavy workloads.
heading: DAX — the cache that only fronts DynamoDB
quote: **DAX serves eventually consistent reads.**

signal: the stem has already decided to cache and the options are caching STRATEGIES (lazy loading / TTL / write-through) — "must never serve stale data"
answer: Write-through (write to cache and DB on every write)
against: Lazy loading plus TTL — TTL only *bounds* staleness, it does not remove it. The cost of write-through is slower writes and caching data nobody reads.
heading: Caching strategies
quote: | **Write-through** | Write to cache **and** DB on every write | Cache always fresh, but writes are slower and you cache data that may never be read |

signal: the options are architectural ("add ElastiCache in front of the DB") and the bottleneck is writes, or a strongly consistent read is required
answer: A cache is the wrong tool — it accelerates reads only
against: "Add ElastiCache in front of the database" offered as the performance fix; lazy loading would happily serve a stale answer.
heading: Worked examples
quote: If the bottleneck is heavy **writes** or the data must be strongly consistent per request, a cache doesn't help (and lazy-loading serves stale data).

signal: "the Redis cluster must fail over automatically" (and the stem describes a single node)
answer: Multi-AZ needs at least one replica — minimum 2 nodes; a single-node cluster cannot fail over
against: Assuming "Redis = HA" from the engine alone; the replica is what makes failover possible, and on cluster mode enabled automatic failover is required rather than optional.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: AWS requires a cluster **with at least one replica** for Multi-AZ, so the **minimum is 2 nodes** — a single-node cluster cannot fail over.

signal: several teams must each process the same events independently, needing a position in a RETAINED LOG: replay, reprocess history, each at its own offset
answer: Kinesis Data Streams (shared log, per-consumer position, replay within retention)
against: SQS deletes a message once processed, so a second consumer never sees it. SNS is the sharper distractor: a FIFO topic with an archive policy *can* replay, so "replay" alone does not kill it — what kills it is many independent consumers each at its own position.
heading: Traps
quote: What eliminates SNS is needing **many independent consumers reading a shared log, each at its own position** — that is Kinesis.

signal: "no code to write" / "just land the streaming data in S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or Splunk"
answer: Amazon Data Firehose
against: Kinesis Data Streams — you would have to write and operate the consumer; the stem explicitly asked for nothing to manage.
heading: Data Streams vs Firehose
quote: | Trigger phrase | "custom processing", "multiple consumers", "replay" | "no code", "just land it in S3/Redshift/OpenSearch/Splunk" |

signal: "the data must be re-readable / consumed again later by another application"
answer: Kinesis Data Streams (24 h – 365 days retention, re-readable)
against: Firehose — it holds undelivered data up to 24 hours while retrying, so it is not literally "no retention", but there is nothing you can read back out of it.
heading: Traps
quote: Firehose has **no readable retention** and no concept of re-reading

signal: "ProvisionedThroughputExceededException at well below the stream's nominal capacity, and adding shards didn't help"
answer: Low-cardinality partition key → hot shard; switch to a high-cardinality key (e.g. device_id)
against: Adding shards or raising the shard count — the key still produces only a handful of hash values, so the new shards stay idle.
heading: Traps
quote: Adding shards does nothing if the partition key only produces a handful of hash values.

signal: "all events for a given customer/device must be processed in the order they arrived"
answer: Give all of that entity's records the same partition key — order is per shard
against: Assuming the stream is globally ordered; two records with different partition keys have no defined relative order. Same mechanic as `MessageGroupId` in FIFO SQS.
heading: Traps
quote: Kinesis guarantees order **within a shard**, not across the stream.

signal: "multiple consumers each need full throughput" / "the consumers are starving each other"
answer: Enhanced fan-out (own 2 MB/sec per shard per registered consumer, pushed via SubscribeToShard)
against: Adding shards — the default shared fan-out splits one shard's 2 MB/sec across every consumer, so more shards does not stop them competing.
heading: Traps
quote: "Multiple consumers each needing full throughput" points at **enhanced fan-out**, not more shards.

signal: "genuinely sub-second, per-record reaction to each event"
answer: Kinesis Data Streams with a consumer (enhanced fan-out if latency really matters)
against: Firehose — but be careful *why*: its buffering interval can be set to 0 seconds ("zero buffering", delivery within a few seconds), so do not eliminate Firehose on latency alone unless the stem demands sub-second per-record handling.
heading: Traps
quote: A requirement for genuinely sub-second, per-record reaction rules it out on its own; that's Data Streams with a consumer, or enhanced fan-out if latency really matters.

signal: "the streaming consumer's IAM role needs DynamoDB permissions" / "unexplained DynamoDB tables appeared"
answer: The Kinesis Client Library stores consumption state in DynamoDB — three tables per application
against: Assuming a Kinesis consumer touches only Kinesis; the DynamoDB dependency is a real IAM requirement, not a distractor.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: **Kinesis Client Library** stores consumption metadata in **DynamoDB** — three tables per application

signal: "reduce our Athena costs" / "the queries scan too much data"
answer: Parquet/ORC + compression + partitioning (plus workgroup scan limits as a guardrail)
against: Any option that resizes something — Athena is serverless and billed on bytes scanned, so there is nothing to make bigger. One caveat: Athena Capacity Reservations ($0.30/DPU-hour) are a real feature, so do not reject an option merely for naming provisioned capacity.
heading: Which engine does the exam mean?
quote: | "reduce Athena cost / scan less data" | **Parquet + compression + partitioning** |

signal: "join years of cold history in S3 to the hot tables already in the warehouse, in one query"
answer: Redshift Spectrum (external schemas/tables over the data catalog)
against: Loading the history into the cluster (expensive, and it was the thing you wanted to avoid) or plain Athena (no warehouse tables to join against).
heading: Which engine does the exam mean?
quote: | "query years of S3 history alongside warehouse tables" | **Redshift Spectrum** |

signal: "full-text search / relevance ranking", "Kibana or OpenSearch Dashboards", "live dashboard of application logs", "real-time monitoring"
answer: Amazon OpenSearch Service
against: Athena — it is SQL aggregates over historical logs already in S3, with nothing running between queries. "Query last quarter's logs with SQL, no infrastructure" flips the answer back to Athena.
heading: Traps
quote: "Search", "index", "Kibana/OpenSearch Dashboards", "real-time monitoring" → OpenSearch.

signal: "use Spot Instances to cut the EMR bill"
answer: Spot for task nodes only; On-Demand for primary and core
against: "Spot for all nodes" — core nodes hold HDFS data so an interruption can lose data, and losing the primary kills the cluster.
heading: Traps
quote: An option offering "Spot for all nodes to save money" is wrong; "Spot for task nodes, On-Demand for primary and core" is the pattern.

signal: "run Spark jobs over S3 with the least operational overhead"
answer: AWS Glue (Spark-based serverless ETL engine)
against: EMR — "Spark" does not automatically mean EMR. EMR wins when the stem wants the wider Hadoop ecosystem, cluster-level control, or Spot economics; it loses on "least operational overhead".
heading: What problem does this solve?
quote: **Glue wins on "Spark + least operational overhead."**

signal: "we already run Kafka" / "must keep our Kafka APIs, tooling and expertise"
answer: Amazon MSK (MSK Serverless if capacity planning is also to go)
against: Kinesis Data Streams — the API is AWS-proprietary, so existing Kafka applications would be rewritten. Greenfield-on-AWS with least overhead flips it back to Kinesis.
heading: Kinesis vs MSK
quote: | Pick it when | greenfield on AWS, least overhead | **existing Kafka** apps, tooling or expertise |

signal: "build a central data repository and import from our RDS databases, bulk then incremental" / "column-level permissions on the data lake"
answer: AWS Lake Formation
against: "Just put it in S3" or hand-written bucket policies — Lake Formation is the authorization layer over the Glue Data Catalog *and* it ingests, which is the half most people miss.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: So "which service builds a centralised data repository and imports from our RDS databases" is **Lake Formation**, not "just put it in S3".

signal: "define the schema once so several query engines can use it" / "discover the schema automatically"
answer: One Glue Crawler into one Glue Data Catalog — shared by Athena, EMR and Redshift Spectrum
against: Options that define schemas per engine or sync metadata between them; that is work AWS already did.
heading: Traps
quote: Athena, EMR and Redshift Spectrum all read the **same AWS Glue Data Catalog**.

signal: "the Redshift warehouse must survive the loss of an entire Region"
answer: Enable cross-Region snapshot copy on the cluster (one destination Region at a time; copies get their own 7-day default retention; KMS clusters need a snapshot copy grant in the destination Region)
against: Automated snapshots alone (they stay in the source Region) or a scheduled job you build — the copy is a cluster configuration, not custom automation.
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: *"You can configure Amazon Redshift to automatically copy snapshots (automated or manual) for a cluster to another AWS Region."*

signal: the root/apex domain (example.com, no www) must point at an ALB or CloudFront
answer: A Route 53 alias record (it resolves as A/AAAA, so the apex rule is never violated)
against: CNAME — DNS forbids a CNAME coexisting with the SOA and NS records the apex must carry, so it is illegal there rather than merely unsupported by AWS
heading: Traps
quote: So a CNAME at the apex is **invalid DNS**, not an AWS limitation.

signal: hand clients several IP addresses but stop handing out the ones that are down
answer: Multivalue answer routing — up to 8 healthy records, randomly ordered
against: Simple routing: it returns all values in random order with no health checking at all, so a dead server keeps being served. Weighted if the stem wants fixed proportions; an ALB if it wants real load balancing
heading: Traps
quote: If the question wants distribution *with* health awareness, it's **multivalue answer**; if it wants controlled proportions, it's **weighted**

signal: each country must be SERVED A DIFFERENT endpoint or site
answer: Geolocation routing — plus a `*` default record so unmatched locations get an answer
against: Geoproximity — it reads where your resources are and offers a bias dial, not where the user is
heading: Traps
quote: If the scenario says "users in Germany must get the German site," that's geolocation.

signal: shift more traffic toward the bigger/closer data centre and tune the share between sites
answer: Geoproximity routing with a bias value (+1…+99 expands, −1…−99 shrinks)
against: Geolocation — it maps user locations to records and has no dial for shifting traffic volume
heading: Traps
quote: If it says "shift more traffic toward the bigger data centre," that's geoproximity bias.

signal: failover record shows healthy in the console, but users kept reaching the dead site for an hour
answer: The record's TTL — lower it (~60s) on failover-critical records
against: Shortening the health check interval or failure threshold: Route 53's own half is ~90s, and the TTL term dominates it
heading: Traps
quote: Route 53 did fail over. The **TTL** kept resolvers and browsers serving the stale answer.

signal: health check a resource that has no public address (an instance in a private subnet)
answer: Health check the public-facing load balancer instead, or use a CloudWatch alarm health check driven by a metric the private resource publishes
against: An endpoint health check pointed at the private IP — Route 53's checkers live on the public internet
heading: Traps
quote: **cannot reach private, nonroutable or multicast addresses**

signal: on-premises DNS servers must resolve names held in AWS (private hosted zones, VPC names)
answer: A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint
against: Outbound endpoint — that is for your VPC resolving on-premises names; anchor on the direction the query travels, not the answer
heading: Traps
quote: **Inbound = traffic coming INTO AWS to be resolved** (on-prem asking about AWS names).

signal: public hosted zone created and the records look right, but the name resolves for nobody on the internet
answer: Point the domain's registrar at the zone's four assigned name servers — the missing NS delegation
against: Editing records, lowering TTLs or adding health checks: that treats a delegation problem as a zone problem
heading: Traps
quote: the registrar must be pointed at the zone's four assigned name servers

signal: a failover record that is an alias to an ALB
answer: Set Evaluate Target Health = Yes on the alias and attach no health check
against: Attaching your own health check to the record — that is only for raw IPs and non-AWS endpoints
heading: Traps
quote: When you create the alias records, you set Evaluate Target Health to Yes instead.

signal: static ANYCAST IPs fronting endpoints in two or more Regions, or non-HTTP (UDP / gaming / VoIP), or failover that must not wait for DNS caches
answer: AWS Global Accelerator — two static anycast IPs, TCP/UDP, caches nothing
against: CloudFront: it caches HTTP at the edge and is reached by DNS name, so a failover still waits for resolver caches to expire
heading: Traps
quote: Trigger words for Global Accelerator: *static IP addresses*, *non-HTTP protocol*, *gaming / VoIP / IoT*, or *failover in seconds without waiting for DNS*.

signal: a globally fast static site where the S3 bucket must stay completely private
answer: OAC on an S3 REST-endpoint origin, plus a bucket policy granting s3:GetObject to cloudfront.amazonaws.com conditioned on AWS:SourceArn = your distribution's ARN
against: The same policy without the condition: everything works, but the service principal is identical for every AWS customer, so any distribution could read the bucket. OAI is the legacy variant
heading: Worked examples
quote: conditioned on `AWS:SourceArn` equal to that distribution's ARN**

signal: CloudFront in front of an S3 bucket configured as a static *website* endpoint, with the bucket required to be private
answer: Switch the origin to the S3 REST endpoint and use OAC, replacing S3's website features with CloudFront's default root object and custom error pages
against: OAC (or OAI) on the website endpoint — a website endpoint is a custom origin and supports neither
heading: Traps
quote: An S3 bucket configured as a **website endpoint** is a **custom origin**, and custom origins support **neither OAC nor OAI**.

signal: a valid ACM certificate never appears in the distribution's certificate list
answer: Request or import the viewer-facing certificate in us-east-1
against: Issuing it in the origin's or your own Region — only the CloudFront→origin leg with an ELB origin may use any Region
heading: Traps
quote: A certificate for **viewer↔CloudFront** HTTPS must be in **`us-east-1`**, regardless of where the origin, the bucket, or you are.

signal: viewers get 502 Bad Gateway from CloudFront
answer: No domain in the origin's certificate matches the origin domain name
against: Treating it as a viewer-certificate or cache problem
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: If no domain in the origin's certificate matches the origin domain name, viewers get **502 Bad Gateway**.

signal: automatic origin failover for an API or a write path (POST/PUT)
answer: Not an origin group — failover happens only for GET, HEAD and OPTIONS viewer requests
against: CloudFront origin groups, which read as the obvious in-CloudFront failover answer
heading: Traps
quote: CloudFront does not fail over when the viewer sends a different HTTP method (for example `POST`, `PUT`, and so on).

signal: edge logic must call another AWS service, use the SDK, or inspect the request body
answer: Lambda@Edge
against: CloudFront Functions — no network access, no request body, viewer events only, 10 KB of code (and it is the right answer for a plain header or URL rewrite at huge scale)
heading: Traps
quote: Anything calling another AWS service, using the SDK, or inspecting a POST body is **Lambda@Edge**.

signal: a CloudFront distribution is already in the architecture and named countries must be DENIED the content (403)
answer: CloudFront geo restriction (allow/block list, applied to the whole distribution, 403 to blocked viewers)
against: Route 53 geolocation routing — it chooses which endpoint a country is sent to, not whether it may access the content
heading: Traps
quote: "Block viewers in country X for licensing reasons" → CloudFront. "Send German users to the German site" → Route 53.

signal: temporary access to private content served THROUGH A CLOUDFRONT DISTRIBUTION
answer: CloudFront signed cookies
against: Signed URLs — one file each, and they change the URLs
heading: Signed URLs vs signed cookies (private content)
quote: you don't want to change your existing URLs

signal: the DR Region already runs a smaller working copy and recovery needs only a scale-up
answer: Warm standby
against: Pilot light — its servers are switched off, so it cannot serve a request until you turn something on
heading: Traps
quote: "Scale up" alone → warm standby. "Turn on, then scale up" → pilot light.

signal: a bad deployment, ransomware or an accidental deletion has already been copied into the DR Region
answer: Point-in-time recovery, versioning or immutable backups (backup & restore is the strategy whose design is an untouched copy)
against: More cross-Region replication — it copies corruption and deletions faithfully, so there is nothing to fail over to
heading: Traps
quote: Any scenario mentioning corruption, ransomware, accidental deletion or a bad release needs **point-in-time recovery, versioning, or immutable backups** — not more replication.

signal: cross-Region recovery for a relational database with sub-minute failover and seconds of data loss
answer: Aurora Global Database
against: RDS cross-Region read replica — promotion takes a few minutes and includes a reboot, which is the planted distractor whenever the RTO/RPO is aggressive
heading: Traps
quote: an RDS read replica promotion takes **a few minutes and includes a reboot**, while Aurora Global Database replicates in **under a second** and promotes in **under a minute**

signal: the MOST resilient failover mechanism during a regional event
answer: Route 53 health checks, or Application Recovery Controller switches — data-plane operations
against: Changing Route 53 weights, moving a Global Accelerator traffic dial, or depending on Auto Scaling to reach capacity: all control plane, and control planes are likeliest to be degraded exactly then
heading: Traps
quote: Route 53 **health checks** and **Application Recovery Controller** are data plane.

signal: data-residency or sovereignty rules confine the workload to a country with only one AWS Region
answer: Implement the same four-strategy choice across that Region's Availability Zones as the discrete locations
against: Concluding DR is impossible, or replicating to a Region in another country and breaking compliance
heading: Traps
quote: the correct answer implements the same strategy across that Region's **Availability Zones**

signal: an aggressive RTO where the alarm itself is slow to fire
answer: Deep health checks against real KPIs — detection, notification, escalation and declaration all sit inside the RTO budget
against: Budgeting the RTO for the failover alone, or a shallow heartbeat that returns 200 while the database is unreachable
heading: Traps
quote: **Detection, notification, escalation, evaluation and declaring the disaster are all inside the RTO.**

signal: a DR game day where the failover worked but the DR Region could not reach production capacity
answer: Pre-provision full capacity (static stability) and raise the DR Region's service quotas ahead of time
against: Tuning the Auto Scaling policy — scaling is the control-plane dependency that caused it, and unraised quotas cap it anyway
heading: Traps
quote: **service quotas in the DR Region that were never raised**

signal: a contractual or SLA-backed replication time for S3 cross-Region replication
answer: S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) — 15 minutes, SLA-backed
against: Plain CRR, which is seconds-to-minutes but carries no commitment
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: **S3 Replication Time Control (RTC)** replicates within **15 minutes**, backed by an SLA

signal: the same job was processed twice, nothing errored, logs look normal
answer: The visibility timeout is shorter than the processing time — raise it (or extend the lease with ChangeMessageVisibility) and make the consumer idempotent
against: A duplicate publish, or switching to FIFO: the cause is that receiving hides a message rather than deleting it
heading: Traps
quote: A received message is **hidden** for the visibility timeout and **comes back** unless the consumer explicitly calls `DeleteMessage`.

signal: one message keeps failing and consumers are stuck looping on it
answer: A dead-letter queue via a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount — and give the DLQ longer retention than the source
against: Raising the retention period or adding consumers; neither puts an upper bound on retries
heading: Traps
quote: Any scenario mentioning messages that repeatedly fail, or a consumer stuck in a loop, is a DLQ question.

signal: empty receives while messages are waiting, wasted API calls, polling cost
answer: Long polling — WaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds
against: Assuming an empty response means an empty queue: short polling is the default and samples only a subset of SQS servers
heading: Traps
quote: If a question mentions empty receives, wasted API calls, or unnecessary cost, the answer is **long polling** with `WaitTimeSeconds` up to **20 seconds**.

signal: one event, several independent consumers, each needing a durable buffer — no replay or ordering asked for; the stated risk is a subscriber being DOWN at delivery time
answer: SNS topic fanning out into one SQS queue per consumer
against: SNS delivering straight to Lambda or an HTTP endpoint — SNS delivers, it does not hold, so a down subscriber loses the notification
heading: Traps
quote: "Must not lose events if a consumer is unavailable" means SNS **into SQS**, not SNS alone.

signal: an existing application already speaking OpenWire, STOMP or AMQP to a broker, and its messaging code must not be rewritten
answer: Amazon MQ
against: SQS/SNS, which speak only the AWS API so adoption means a rewrite — and note that MQTT telemetry from constrained devices points at IoT Core, not MQ
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: If a scenario names a **broker/JMS** protocol — **OpenWire, STOMP, AMQP** — beside an existing broker-based application, the answer is Amazon MQ

signal: three broker nodes behind a Network Load Balancer across Availability Zones
answer: Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ, cluster deployment (each node on its own EBS volume)
against: ActiveMQ active/standby — that is two brokers in two AZs on shared EFS; RabbitMQ has no active/standby mode and no EFS option
heading: Traps
quote: So "three brokers / cluster / NLB" is a RabbitMQ stem, and "two brokers, one active, shared EFS" is an ActiveMQ stem.

signal: an S3 event notification must end up in a FIFO queue
answer: Put EventBridge in the middle — S3 cannot name a FIFO queue (or an SNS FIFO topic) as an event-notification destination
against: Configuring the FIFO queue directly as the S3 event destination
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: So S3 → FIFO needs **EventBridge** in the middle.

signal: ingest events natively from a third-party SaaS provider
answer: EventBridge — partner event sources and custom event buses
against: SNS: it can push notifications *out* to third-party providers but cannot ingest a SaaS partner's events; the direction is the discriminator
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: A stem about decoupling from a **SaaS provider's events** is EventBridge

signal: scale a queue-consumer fleet to meet a stated latency SLA ("process within N seconds")
answer: Target-track on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage
against: Backlog per instance (right for keeping up with throughput, not for a latency SLA) and consumer CPU (an I/O-blocked consumer shows no CPU while the backlog grows)
heading: Scaling the consumers on the queue itself
quote: a stated **latency SLA** | **`ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage`**

signal: alarm on memory utilisation, swap, or free disk space on EC2
answer: Install the CloudWatch agent; those arrive as custom metrics
against: Enabling detailed monitoring — it changes the frequency (5 min → 1 min), never the set of metrics
heading: ⚠️ Traps — why the wrong answer looks right
quote: Any stem that wants memory, swap, or free disk space needs the **CloudWatch agent**, and those arrive as **custom metrics**.

signal: which user or role made this API call / who deleted it
answer: CloudTrail
against: Config — it shows what the resource looked like before and after, but never the caller
heading: The four services — the discrimination the exam actually tests
quote: "**Who** deleted it", "which user/role made this API call", "audit for compliance"

signal: was this resource ever non-compliant during a past period / prove the configuration over time
answer: AWS Config — configuration items versioned over time, plus rules (and SSM Automation remediation)
against: CloudTrail: it records that `PutBucketAcl` was called, not what the ACL then was
heading: ⚠️ Traps — why the wrong answer looks right
quote: "Was this bucket public at any point last quarter?" or "produce evidence that all volumes have been encrypted since January" is **AWS Config**

signal: notify the team when a specific string appears in the application log
answer: Metric filter on the log group → custom metric → metric alarm → SNS
against: An alarm on the log group itself: alarms watch metrics, so the metric filter is the missing middle step
heading: Worked examples
quote: The chain is log line → metric filter → metric → alarm → SNS.

signal: audit who read or wrote individual S3 objects (or who invoked a Lambda)
answer: Configure data events (an event selector) on a trail — they are opt-in and billed by volume
against: "Enable CloudTrail" alone, or the free 90-day Event history, which covers management events only
heading: ⚠️ Traps — why the wrong answer looks right
quote: Object-level reads and writes are **data events**

signal: retain audit logs for seven years for compliance
answer: A trail delivering to S3, with S3 lifecycle to cheaper storage
against: CloudTrail Event history — that is 90 days, per Region, management events only, and is a console view not a retention setting
heading: ⚠️ Traps — why the wrong answer looks right
quote: A stem wanting "retain audit logs for seven years for compliance" is asking for a trail plus S3 lifecycle, not the console view.

signal: instance unreachable because of a fault on the underlying host (power, network, hardware)
answer: A CloudWatch alarm action `recover` on StatusCheckFailed_System — it moves the instance to new hardware, keeping its instance ID and every IP including the public IPv4
against: `reboot`, which keeps the instance on the same broken host; and `recover` wired to StatusCheckFailed_Instance, which AWS does not permit. RAM contents are lost either way, and a terminated instance can never be recovered
heading: ⚠️ Traps — why the wrong answer looks right
quote: A reboot keeps the instance on the **same broken host**, so it fixes nothing

signal: install a third-party tool on hundreds of instances once, now, without SSH or RDP
answer: Systems Manager Run Command
against: Patch Manager (it updates existing software against a baseline), Maintenance Windows (it only says *when*, it never performs the work), State Manager (it holds a state over time, wrong for a one-off)
heading: Which Systems Manager tool — the discrimination that actually gets tested
quote: | **Run Command** | run a command or script across a fleet **once, now**, without logging in |

signal: shell access to an instance in a private subnet with no bastion, no inbound port and no SSH key — and sessions must be auditable
answer: Systems Manager Session Manager, logging to S3 or CloudWatch Logs (plus interface VPC endpoints when the subnet has no internet access at all)
against: A bastion/jump host, an inbound SSH rule from the corporate CIDR, or distributing key pairs — all three are the old answer and all three are listed as distractors
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: gives *"secure node management without the need to open inbound ports, maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys"*

signal: notify the security team 30 days before an *imported* third-party certificate expires, with least effort
answer: The AWS Config managed rule `acm-certificate-expiration-check` plus SNS (ACM does not auto-renew imported certificates)
against: Eliminating Config on principle — that is only right when the option describes a *custom* rule you must write. For ACM-issued certificates the DaysToExpiry alarm or an EventBridge rule on AWS Health events is the direct answer
heading: ⚠️ Traps — why the wrong answer looks right
quote: `acm-certificate-expiration-check` is a real AWS Config managed rule

signal: the alarm must trigger an Auto Scaling or EC2 action
answer: A metric alarm
against: A composite alarm — it exists to reduce alarm noise and cannot perform EC2 or Auto Scaling actions, only SNS
heading: ⚠️ Traps — why the wrong answer looks right
quote: If the stem needs a scaling action, the alarm doing it must be a metric alarm.

signal: notify us automatically when somebody calls a specific API, with the least machinery
answer: An EventBridge rule on the `AWS API Call via CloudTrail` detail-type targeting SNS — with a trail actively logging, the rule in the Region where the call happens, and `ENABLED_WITH_ALL_CLOUDTRAIL_MANAGEMENT_EVENTS` if the call is read-only
against: Shipping CloudTrail logs to S3 and querying with Athena, or a Lambda poller — both far heavier for "tell us when X happens"
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: rules on the detail-type **`AWS API Call via CloudTrail`** (source `aws.<service>`) fire on a specific `eventSource` and `eventName`

signal: run a containerised job when an event fires, or on a schedule
answer: An EventBridge rule targeting the ECS task directly (mapped through to ecs.RunTask)
against: A Lambda in between whose only job is to call RunTask — that is the distractor
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: needs **no Lambda in between**; a Lambda that only calls `RunTask` is a distractor.

signal: the alarm sits in INSUFFICIENT_DATA and almost never evaluates on an EC2 instance
answer: The alarm period is shorter than the metric's resolution — use 300s, or enable detailed monitoring
against: Changing the threshold; and for a metric that simply stops publishing when idle, the fix is the missing-data treatment instead
heading: Worked examples
quote: select an alarm monitoring period that is greater than or equal to the metrics resolution.

signal: pull totals, fields or tables out of scanned invoices, forms or contracts
answer: Amazon Textract (AnalyzeExpense for invoices and receipts)
against: Rekognition — it reads scenes and text *in a picture of the world*, and does not preserve document structure or key-value pairs
heading: Traps
quote: **If the subject is a document — an invoice, a form, a tax return, a contract — it's Textract**

signal: add the capability "without machine learning expertise", "fully managed", "minimal development effort" or "as quickly as possible"
answer: The matching pre-trained AI service — one API call, no model
against: SageMaker: correct only when the stem asks for a custom model trained on the company's own data, and its always-on endpoint contradicts any low-cost/low-overhead framing
heading: Traps
quote: SageMaker is the distractor and a pre-trained API is the answer.

signal: employees ask natural-language questions of internal documents
answer: Amazon Kendra
against: Comprehend (it analyses text for sentiment/entities/PII and returns no ranked results) and OpenSearch (a keyword index and log-dashboard engine you size and run)
heading: Kendra vs OpenSearch
quote: "employees ask questions of internal docs" | "search index", "log dashboards", "Kibana"

signal: multi-page PDFs or long audio processed from a Lambda
answer: The asynchronous job API plus an SNS completion notification
against: Calling the synchronous API — it handles single-page documents only, and Lambda's timeout kills the design on real input
heading: Traps
quote: Textract's synchronous operations handle **single-page** documents only; multi-page PDFs require the **asynchronous** API

signal: filter inappropriate or explicit user-uploaded images
answer: Rekognition content moderation — one API call
against: A SageMaker project to train an image classifier: it sounds like the serious answer and rebuilds a pre-trained feature
heading: Worked examples
quote: to rebuild **Rekognition content moderation**, which is one API call and needs no model at all

signal: a call-centre stem that already uses Transcribe Call Analytics and wants speaker sentiment
answer: Call Analytics already produces speaker sentiment natively
against: Adding Comprehend — that is the over-built answer here, and is only required with plain Transcribe or Transcribe Medical
heading: Worked examples
quote: **Call Analytics** → it is already included, and adding Comprehend is the over-built distractor.

signal: time-series demand or inventory prediction, with Amazon Forecast among the options
answer: Amazon Forecast is still the intended answer
against: Talking yourself out of it because the service is closed to new customers — it remains in the exam guide's in-scope list
heading: Traps
quote: If a question describes time-series demand prediction and offers **Amazon Forecast**, that is still the intended answer

signal: move a large on-premises Oracle database to Aurora PostgreSQL with only minutes of downtime
answer: AWS SCT (or DMS Schema Conversion) for the schema, then DMS full load plus ongoing replication (CDC) until cutover
against: DMS alone — it moves data, not schema, so it is complete only when source and target run the same engine; and "export a dump and restore it" blows the downtime budget at that size
heading: AWS DMS — the migration answer, and the biggest gap here
quote: **SCT to convert the schema, then DMS with ongoing replication to move the data and keep it current until cutover.**

signal: continuously consolidate several live RDS databases into a data warehouse, least development effort, no infrastructure to manage
answer: DMS with Redshift as the target (CDC natively)
against: Glue (batch ETL and a catalogue, not change data capture), EMR (a cluster the stem did not want), Kinesis Data Streams (producers and consumers you still write)
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: DMS → Redshift beats Glue/EMR for *continuous replication into a warehouse*.

signal: replication volume that varies or spikes, with least operational overhead
answer: DMS Serverless — a replication configuration that auto-provisions and auto-scales
against: A sized DMS replication instance, which leaves you doing capacity estimation and engine patching
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: Trigger: spiky/variable volume + least operational overhead.

signal: a workflow that pauses for a human approval that may take days, and every step must be auditable
answer: Step Functions Standard, using Wait for Callback (.waitForTaskToken)
against: Express — capped at five minutes, Request Response only (no .waitForTaskToken), and never exactly-once
heading: Traps
quote: "Human approval" in a question is effectively a Standard flag.

signal: one client call must read and write across several DynamoDB tables, most operationally efficient, without hurting baseline performance
answer: An AppSync pipeline resolver (functions chained server-side, each against a data source)
against: A Lambda behind API Gateway fanning out (you write the logic, heavier ops), Athena Federated Query (analytical SQL, far too slow for a request path), CloudFront Functions (cannot reach DynamoDB at all)
heading: AWS AppSync — managed GraphQL
quote: The server-side-chaining answer is an **AppSync pipeline resolver**.

signal: the API style is GraphQL, or a mobile app needs real-time data and offline sync
answer: AWS AppSync (subscriptions over serverless WebSockets; Amplify is built on it)
against: API Gateway — REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs, not GraphQL
heading: AWS AppSync — managed GraphQL
quote: REST/HTTP/WebSocket → API Gateway; **GraphQL → AppSync**.

signal: a containerised job that runs for hours (genomics, rendering, simulation), ideally on Spot
answer: AWS Batch
against: Lambda — answer 15 minutes as the exam's ceiling. Inverse trap: a short, spiky, event-driven workload put on Batch is over-engineering, because Batch has queue and provisioning latency
heading: AWS Batch — containerised batch jobs at any scale
quote: "Nightly job that takes four hours" is Batch, not Lambda.

signal: tightly coupled HPC with MPI AND the options are services that RUN the job — "one submission", "gang scheduling", "minimal operational overhead"
answer: AWS Batch multi-node parallel jobs (gang scheduling, one submission, a main node plus children)
against: An Auto Scaling group, a CloudFormation-managed cluster placement group, or Elastic Beanstalk — all leave you building the coordination
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: So **tightly coupled MPI HPC with minimal operational overhead** is Batch MNP

signal: external partners upload over SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2 and cannot change their clients
answer: AWS Transfer Family, landing files directly in S3 or EFS
against: DataSync — a transfer job you run to move a dataset between storage systems, not a standing protocol endpoint. If the stem names a protocol, it is Transfer Family
heading: Traps
quote: If the question names a **protocol**, it's Transfer Family.

signal: B2B/EDI file exchange with supply-chain, payments or ERP partners
answer: AS2 on AWS Transfer Family
against: SFTP/FTPS, which carry no EDI framing, and DataSync, which speaks none of these protocols
heading: AWS Transfer Family — SFTP as a managed service
quote: **AS2** is the one to recognise separately — it's the B2B/EDI protocol, so supply-chain, payments and ERP integration scenarios point at it.

signal: the directory must work with Amazon RDS for SQL Server (or needs trusts, schema extensions, LDAPS or MFA)
answer: AWS Managed Microsoft AD
against: AD Connector and Simple AD — both explicitly incompatible with RDS for SQL Server, and Simple AD supports none of trusts, schema extensions, LDAPS or MFA
heading: Traps
quote: **Only AWS Managed Microsoft AD works with Amazon RDS for SQL Server.**

signal: on-premises users must sign in with existing credentials AND the options are the three Directory Service flavours — the axis is where the user records live
answer: AD Connector — a proxy that forwards sign-in requests to your on-premises domain controllers
against: Managed Microsoft AD (a real directory in AWS, more than asked) and Simple AD (a standalone Samba 4 directory, which stores its own users)
heading: AWS Directory Service — three options, one real discriminator
quote: sign-in requests are **forwarded to your existing on-premises domain controllers** for authentication

signal: a SaaS or consumer application's own end users, social sign-in, scaling to millions
answer: Amazon Cognito
against: Directory Service in any flavour — that is workforce identity for employees and domain-joined machines
heading: Traps
quote: For a **consumer or SaaS application's own users**, including social sign-in and scaling to millions, the answer is **Amazon Cognito**.

signal: after signing in, the mobile app calls S3 or DynamoDB directly — or needs guest/unauthenticated access
answer: A Cognito identity pool, which exchanges a trusted token for temporary AWS credentials via STS
against: A user pool alone — it authenticates people and issues JWTs but mints no AWS credentials (the ALB's built-in Cognito authentication is also a user-pool integration)
heading: Amazon Cognito — two pools that do different jobs
quote: it needs **AWS credentials**, and only an **identity pool** mints those.

signal: authenticate users before the request ever reaches the application servers
answer: An Application Load Balancer listener rule with built-in Cognito user pool authentication
against: Building auth into the application, or an identity pool, which has no part in that integration
heading: Amazon Cognito — two pools that do different jobs
quote: built-in **Cognito user pool** authentication

signal: deploy the same baseline into many accounts and Regions in one operation
answer: CloudFormation StackSets (from an admin account or via Organizations)
against: Running the template per account by hand; and for "let teams self-serve only pre-approved configurations" the answer is Service Catalog, not raw CloudFormation
heading: AWS CloudFormation — the standardisation answer
quote: deploy one template across **many accounts and Regions in a single operation**

signal: keep (or snapshot) a database when its CloudFormation stack is deleted
answer: A `DeletionPolicy` of `Retain`, or `Snapshot` to take one first
against: Relying on the default, which is `Delete`
heading: AWS CloudFormation — the standardisation answer
quote: default is **Delete**; `Retain` keeps it, `Snapshot` takes one first (RDS, EBS and friends)

signal: deploy a web app quickly with minimal setup while keeping control of the EC2 instances, ASG and load balancer, at no extra service cost
answer: Elastic Beanstalk
against: Rejecting it over an imagined service charge or because it "hides" the infrastructure — it is free and the resources stay in your account; a fully managed container service is the genuinely more abstracted option
heading: Traps
quote: **Beanstalk itself is free — you pay only for the EC2, ELB and other resources it creates**

signal: containerise an existing commercial off-the-shelf application with no source code available
answer: AWS App2Container — it inspects the running app and generates OCI images
against: App Runner, which is only a runtime: it runs an image or an already-buildable repo and cannot containerise anything
heading: Key facts, limits & pricing
quote: does not need source code for the application to containerize it
